subject: system-design
title: Content Delivery Network (CDN)
summary: A mesh of edge servers spread around the world that caches content near users to cut latency and shield the origin from load.

blocks.text: A CDN is a geographically distributed network of caching servers that hold copies of your content close to where users are. Instead of every request crossing the globe to your origin, a user in Tokyo is served from a nearby edge in Tokyo. The result is lower latency for users and far less traffic reaching your origin.
Points of presence at the edge

The caching servers live in points of presence (PoPs), which are data centers scattered across cities and regions. Each PoP keeps a local copy of popular content, so most requests are answered a few network hops away rather than from a single distant origin. More PoPs, closer to more users, means lower round-trip times.

items: Pull CDN: the edge fetches content from the origin on the first miss, then caches it. The origin is the source of truth and you do nothing to populate the edge.
Push CDN: you upload content to the CDN ahead of time and it serves what you pushed. This gives more control and is good for large files you know will be requested.
Pull is the common default; push suits rarely-changing bulk assets where a first-request miss would be costly.

blocks.text: Each cached object carries a time-to-live (TTL) that says how long the edge may serve it before re-checking the origin. A long TTL maximizes cache hits but risks serving stale content; a short TTL keeps content fresh but pushes more traffic back to the origin. When you must change something before its TTL expires, you issue an explicit purge or invalidation, or bust the cache by versioning the URL (for example, a content hash in the filename).
Routing users to the nearest edge

Getting each user to a close PoP is itself a routing problem. DNS-based routing resolves the CDN hostname to the IP of a nearby edge based on the resolver's location. Anycast advertises the same IP from many PoPs and lets the network's routing deliver the request to the topologically nearest one. Both steer users to a good edge without the client knowing the topology.

CDNs shine for static, cacheable assets: images, CSS, JavaScript, fonts, and especially video, where edge delivery and segmenting dominate the experience. They also offer dynamic acceleration for non-cacheable requests: terminating TLS at the edge and carrying traffic to the origin over optimized backbone routes shaves latency even when the response itself can't be cached.

blocks.title: Two wins at once
blocks.text: A CDN does double duty: it lowers user-perceived latency by serving from nearby, and it shields the origin by absorbing the bulk of requests at the edge. The same cache hit that makes a page fast also keeps a request off your servers. Reach for one whenever you serve cacheable content to a wide geography. But remember its cache leaks the usual way, through staleness, so design TTLs and invalidation deliberately.
